projects.subject: physics
projects.title: The Crane Cable That Never Came Back
projects.mission: After one rapid hoist, a tower crane's steel cable was found permanently longer. Slow lifts never caused this. Investigate why a fast hoist behaves differently, measure the stress and stretch in the cable, and choose a replacement cable for heavier beams without wasting money.

learningCapsule.title: Tension, Stress, Strain and the Elastic Limit

sections.title: Tension when a load accelerates
sections.content: A hanging load of mass m moves upward with acceleration a. Newton's second law gives T − mg = ma, so the cable tension is T = m(g + a). At constant speed a = 0 and the tension equals the weight.

sections.title: Stress, strain and Young's modulus
sections.content: Stress is force per unit cross-sectional area, σ = F/A. Strain is the fractional change in length, ε = ΔL/L. Within the elastic range, Young's modulus Y = σ/ε is a constant for the material, so the extension is ΔL = (σ/Y) × L.

sections.title: The elastic limit
sections.content: Below the elastic limit, a material returns to its original length when the load is removed. Above it, part of the stretch becomes permanent. A design must keep the peak stress, not just the average stress, below this limit.

levels.title: Why Did Only the Fast Hoist Damage the Cable?

questions.prompt: The incident report says slow, steady lifts of the beam leave the cable's length unchanged, but one rapid hoist left the cable permanently longer. Which explanation should the team investigate first?
options: During the rapid hoist the cable stress became larger and crossed the elastic limit.
The beam became lighter during the rapid hoist.
Steel stops obeying Newton's laws at high hoisting speeds.
The cable's Young's modulus changed during the hoist.
questions.answer: During the rapid hoist the cable stress became larger and crossed the elastic limit.
questions.explanation: Permanent stretch means the elastic limit was exceeded. Steady lifts stayed below it. The difference between the two cases is the upward acceleration, which increases the tension and therefore the stress.
hints: What is different about the rapid hoist compared with steady lifts?
Permanent stretch is linked to a particular property of the material. Which one?

questions.prompt: A beam of fixed mass hangs from the cable. How does the cable tension during an upward acceleration compare with the tension during a constant-speed lift?
options: The tension is larger during the upward acceleration.
The tension is the same in both cases.
The tension is smaller during the upward acceleration.
The tension is zero during a constant-speed lift.
questions.answer: The tension is larger during the upward acceleration.
questions.explanation: For upward acceleration, T − mg = ma, so T = m(g + a), which is greater than mg. At constant speed T = mg.
hints: Draw the forces on the beam: tension upward and weight downward.
If the beam is accelerating upward, which force must be larger?

levels.evidenceUse: Read crane_incident_report.txt and compare the steady lifts with the rapid hoist.
levels.simulationUse: Raise the hoist acceleration in the simulation and watch how tension and stress change.

levels.title: Measure the Stress and the Stretch

questions.prompt: Using the figures in the incident report for the rapid hoist, what was the tension in the cable? Take g = 10 m/s².
hints: The load was accelerating upward, so the tension is more than the weight.
Apply Newton's second law to the beam.

questions.prompt: Cable A has a cross-sectional area of 1.0 cm², which is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m². What stress did the rapid hoist produce in the cable?
questions.explanation: σ = F/A = 28 000 / (1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.8 × 10⁸ Pa = 280 MPa. This is above the elastic limit of 250 MPa, which explains the permanent stretch.
hints: Stress compares the force with the area that carries it.
Convert square centimetres to square metres before dividing.

questions.prompt: During a steady, constant-speed lift of the same 2000 kg beam, the 50 m cable stays within its elastic range. By how much does Cable A stretch during that steady lift?
questions.explanation: Steady tension = mg = 20 000 N, so stress = 20 000 / (1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 2.0 × 10⁸ Pa. Strain = stress / Y = 2.0 × 10⁸ / 2.0 × 10¹¹ = 1.0 × 10⁻³. Extension = strain × length = 1.0 × 10⁻³ × 50 = 0.05 m = 5 cm.
hints: At constant speed the tension equals the weight.
Find the stress, then use Young's modulus to find the strain.
Extension is strain multiplied by the original length.

levels.evidenceUse: Use the cable area and length from crane_incident_report.txt and Young's modulus from cable_material_standard.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Compare your tension, stress and extension values with the simulation readouts.

levels.title: Test Thicker Cables

questions.prompt: Cable A is replaced by a cable of the same steel with twice the cross-sectional area. The load and acceleration are unchanged. What happens to the stress in the cable?
options: The stress becomes half as large.
The stress becomes twice as large.
The stress does not change.
The stress becomes four times smaller.
questions.answer: The stress becomes half as large.
questions.explanation: The tension stays the same but is shared over twice the area. Since σ = F/A, the stress becomes half as large.
hints: Which quantities in the stress relationship stay fixed, and which one changed?

questions.prompt: Cable D has a cross-sectional area of 2.0 cm² and the same length and material as Cable A. How much does it stretch during the rapid hoist of the 2000 kg beam?
hints: The tension in the rapid hoist is the same as before.
Find the new stress, then the strain, then the extension.

questions.prompt: The cable catalogue lists Cables A, B, C and D with different cross-sectional areas. Considering the rapid hoist of the 2000 kg beam, which cables would have stayed within the elastic limit?
options: Cables B, C and D only
Cable D only
All four cables
Cable A only
questions.answer: Cables B, C and D only
questions.explanation: The tension is 28 000 N and the elastic limit is 250 MPa, so the area must be at least 28 000 / (2.5 × 10⁸) = 1.12 × 10⁻⁴ m² = 1.12 cm². Cable A (1.0 cm²) fails with 280 MPa. Cable B (1.2 cm²) gives about 233 MPa, and C and D give lower stresses.
hints: Find the smallest area that keeps the stress at or below the elastic limit.
Compare that area with the catalogue.

levels.evidenceUse: Use cable_options.csv together with the elastic limit in cable_material_standard.txt.
levels.simulationUse: Switch between cable areas in the simulation and note which ones stay below the elastic limit.

levels.title: Choose the Cable for Heavier Beams

questions.prompt: For the upcoming job, the crane must hoist the heavier beams with the maximum upward acceleration in the standard. What is the minimum cable cross-sectional area that keeps the stress at or below the elastic limit?
hints: Start with the tension for the heavier beam at the maximum acceleration.
The stress must not exceed the elastic limit. Solve the stress relationship for area.

questions.prompt: The site already owns a spare Cable B (1.2 cm²). If it is used for the 2500 kg beams, what is the largest upward acceleration that keeps the stress at or below the elastic limit? Take g = 10 m/s².
hints: Find the largest tension the cable can carry without reaching the elastic limit.
Then work backwards from the tension to the acceleration.

questions.prompt: The schedule requires hoisting the 2500 kg beams with the full maximum acceleration. The cable must keep the stress at or below the elastic limit, keep the peak extension within the extension limit, and cost as little as possible. Which cable should be purchased?
options: Cable A: 1.0 cm², ₹400 per metre
Cable B: 1.2 cm², ₹480 per metre
Cable C: 1.5 cm², ₹600 per metre
Cable D: 2.0 cm², ₹800 per metre
questions.explanation: The tension is 35 000 N. Cable A gives 350 MPa and Cable B gives about 292 MPa, both above the 250 MPa limit. Cable C gives about 233 MPa and an extension of about 5.8 cm, within the 6 cm limit. Cable D also satisfies both limits but costs more per metre, so Cable C is the cheapest valid choice.
hints: Check the stress limit first. It removes some cables immediately.
For the remaining cables, check the extension limit, then compare cost.

levels.evidenceUse: Use cable_material_standard.txt for the new job details and limits, and cable_options.csv for areas and prices.
levels.simulationUse: Test the heavier load and maximum acceleration with each cable before submitting the final choice.

requiredEvidence.instruction: Read every required file and use its information while solving the mission. The evidence is part of the investigation.

files.purpose: Read what happened during the steady lifts and the rapid hoist, and the details of Cable A.
files.content: Tower crane lifting steel beams. Steady (constant-speed) lifts of a 2000 kg beam leave the cable's length unchanged afterwards. During one rapid hoist, the 2000 kg beam accelerated upward at 4 m/s² and the cable was found permanently longer afterwards. Cable A: steel, length 50 m, cross-sectional area 1.0 cm² (1.0 × 10⁻⁴ m²). Use g = 10 m/s².

files.purpose: Read Young's modulus, the elastic limit, the extension limit and the requirements of the upcoming job.
files.content: Young's modulus of the cable steel: 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Elastic limit (stress above which stretch becomes permanent): 2.5 × 10⁸ Pa. Cable length on this crane: 50 m. Maximum permitted extension at peak load: 6 cm. Upcoming job: 2500 kg beams, hoisted with upward acceleration up to 4 m/s² when the schedule is tight. Use g = 10 m/s².

files.purpose: Compare the cross-sectional area and price of each available cable.

requiredSimulation.description: Interactive physics simulation of a crane hoisting a steel beam. Controls: beam mass, upward acceleration, cable cross-sectional area and cable length. It displays tension, stress, strain, extension, the elastic limit and an elastic / permanent-stretch status.
requiredSimulation.integrationComment: Use the simulation to see how acceleration raises tension and stress, to compare cable areas, and to test the heavier-beam job against the stress and extension limits before choosing a cable.
